group.title: Relationships
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: The way two people or groups feel and behave toward each other.
examples: She has a good {relationship} with her boss.
wrong: A relationship is a building where people work.

words.meaning: The person you live with or are in a relationship with.
examples: My {partner} and I met at college.
wrong: My partner is a stranger I have never met.

words.meaning: Having agreed to marry someone.
examples: They got {engaged} last summer.
wrong: They are engaged, so they never plan to marry.

words.meaning: The legal end of a marriage.
examples: Her parents got a {divorce} last year.
wrong: A divorce is the day two people get married.

words.meaning: A ceremony where two people get married.
examples: We danced all night at the {wedding}.
wrong: A wedding is the end of a marriage.

words.meaning: A relationship between friends.
examples: Their {friendship} began at school.
wrong: Friendship is a feeling of hate between two people.

words.meaning: An angry talk between people who disagree.
examples: They had an {argument} about money.
wrong: An argument is a quiet talk where everyone agrees.

words.meaning: Words that say you are sorry.
examples: I owe you an {apology}.
wrong: An apology is a way of saying thank you.

words.meaning: A feeling that someone is good and important.
examples: Children should show {respect} to their teachers.
wrong: He has respect for her, so he is always rude to her.

words.meaning: To trust someone or something to help you.
examples: You can always {rely on} me.
wrong: I rely on him, so I never trust him with anything.

words.meaning: To have a friendly relationship.
examples: I {get along} well with my sister.
wrong: We get along, so we argue all the time.

words.meaning: To stop being friends after an argument.
examples: They {fell out} over a small thing.
wrong: We fell out, so we became best friends.

words.meaning: To end a romantic relationship.
examples: They {broke up} after two years.
wrong: They broke up and got married the next day.

words.meaning: To keep talking to or writing to someone.
examples: Let’s {keep in touch} after the course.
wrong: We keep in touch, so we never speak.

words.meaning: To become friends again after an argument.
examples: They argued, but they {made up} the next day.
wrong: We made up, so we are still angry with each other.

words.meaning: Knowing someone very well and liking them a lot.
examples: We are very {close} friends.
wrong: We are close friends, so we hardly know each other.

words.meaning: Always supporting your friends or beliefs.
examples: My dog is very {loyal}.
wrong: He is loyal, so he left his friends when things got hard.

words.meaning: To go out with someone in a romantic way.
examples: They {dated} for a year before they married.
wrong: They dated, but they never met.

words.meaning: Pleasant to look at.
examples: He thinks she is very {attractive}.
wrong: She is attractive, so nobody likes to look at her.

words.meaning: Connected with love.
examples: They had a {romantic} dinner by candlelight.
wrong: The dinner was romantic, so it was about business.

words.meaning: Talk about other people’s private lives.
examples: Don’t listen to office {gossip}.
wrong: Gossip is serious news from the government.

words.meaning: A story that may not be true, passed from person to person.
examples: There’s a {rumor} that the shop will close.
wrong: A rumor is a fact that everyone has checked.

words.meaning: Something that you do not tell other people.
examples: Can you keep a {secret}?
wrong: A secret is something that everyone knows.

words.meaning: To say that you will certainly do something.
examples: I {promise} I’ll be on time.
wrong: I promised to come, so I told her I might not.

words.meaning: To feel sad because someone is not with you.
examples: I {miss} my family when I travel.
wrong: I miss her, so I’m glad she’s gone.

words.meaning: The time when you are a child.
examples: I had a happy {childhood} in the country.
wrong: My childhood was when I was sixty.

words.meaning: All the people born at about the same time.
examples: My parents’ {generation} didn’t have phones.
wrong: A generation is one person in a family.

words.meaning: A person you know a little, but not well.
examples: He’s an {acquaintance}, not a close friend.
wrong: An acquaintance is my best friend since birth.

words.meaning: A strong feeling that connects people.
examples: There is a strong {bond} between the twins.
wrong: A bond is a feeling that keeps people apart.

words.meaning: Help and kindness that you give someone.
examples: Thanks for your {support} after the accident.
wrong: She gave me support by laughing at my problem.

words.meaning: To feel that something or someone is important.
examples: I really {care} about my friends.
wrong: I care about her, so I don’t mind what happens to her.

words.meaning: Able to be trusted.
examples: She is honest and {trustworthy}.
wrong: He is trustworthy, so he always lies to his friends.

words.meaning: A person you share a flat with.
examples: My {flatmate} cooks dinner on Fridays.
wrong: A flatmate is a person who lives in another country and never visits.

words.meaning: A woman on her wedding day.
examples: The {bride} wore a long white dress.
wrong: The bride is the man she marries.

words.meaning: A feeling of being sorry for someone who is sad or in trouble.
examples: We sent our {sympathy} to the family.
wrong: She showed sympathy by laughing at his bad news.

words.meaning: To say that someone has done well.
examples: The teacher {praised} her work.
wrong: He praised me by saying my work was terrible.

words.meaning: To say that someone is responsible for something bad.
examples: Don’t {blame} me; it wasn’t my fault.
wrong: I blamed him for the gift he kindly gave me.

words.meaning: Responsibility for a mistake.
examples: The accident was not your {fault}.
wrong: It was my fault, so I had nothing to do with it.

words.meaning: To act in a certain way.
examples: The children {behaved} well at the party.
wrong: He behaved badly, so everyone thanked him.

words.meaning: To laugh at someone in a friendly or unkind way.
examples: My brother always {teases} me about my hair.
wrong: He teased me by saying nothing at all.
